opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a really interesting question, because those are exactly the domains where the "just scrape the internet" playbook breaks down. For language, we got incredibly lucky. Humanity spent decades writing everything down and putting it online, so there was this enormous pre-existing corpus sitting there waiting for us. That isn't true for something like cancer research or robotics.

In cancer research, the data exists in some sense, but it's fragmented. It's locked inside hospital systems, it's subject to privacy constraints, it's labeled inconsistently, and a lot of the most valuable signal, like longitudinal outcomes and what happened to a patient five years after a given treatment, is sparse and expensive to collect. So the bottleneck isn't really compute or architecture. It's access, and it's the fact that the experiments that generate new knowledge happen in wet labs and clinical trials, which run on biological time, not GPU time.

Robotics has a different version of the same problem. There's no internet of robot actions. Every demonstration has to be physically collected, the embodiments differ from one lab to the next, and the real world is slow and unforgiving. You can't run a million parallel trials of a robot arm folding laundry the way you can sample a million completions from a language model.

So I think a few things happen. First, synthetic data and simulation become much more important. We've already seen in language that models can generate useful training data for themselves, especially when you have a way to verify the output. In robotics, sim-to-real is getting better, and in biology, models that can propose hypotheses or simulate molecular interactions can help you prioritize which expensive experiments are actually worth running.

Second, I think the general models become the foundation. A strong language model already carries a huge amount of compressed knowledge about biology, chemistry, and physics from the literature. You don't need to learn everything from scratch with domain data. You need a smaller amount of high-quality domain data to specialize something that already understands the world reasonably well.

And third, I think the people who solve the data collection and partnership problems will have a real advantage, more than the people with marginally better models. Whoever can work with hospitals, pharma companies, or fleets of deployed robots and build that data flywheel in a responsible way is going to unlock a lot.

But I'd be honest that it's going to be slower than what we saw in language. The feedback loops are physical, and physics doesn't scale like software does.

r001.rationale: The response says cancer data exists “in some sense,” but describes it as fragmented and sparse. For robotics, it says demonstrations must be physically collected and that there is no internet of robot actions. It does not state that sufficient data already exists across both domains.

r002.rationale: The response says cancer data is locked in hospital systems and subject to privacy constraints, but does not say data holders refuse to share it. It gives no equivalent claim about robotics.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, I think this is actually one of the most underappreciated things about where we are right now. The reason language models got so good so fast is that we had this enormous, free, pre-existing dataset: the internet. Humanity had already spent decades writing everything down. We didn't have to generate that data; we just had to go collect it and learn from it.

But that's a very special situation, and most domains don't look like that. If you look at something like cancer research, the data you actually need is high-fidelity, it's often messy, it sits inside hospitals and labs under all sorts of privacy and regulatory constraints, and in many cases it just doesn't exist yet. There's no "internet of oncology" where every experiment, every patient trajectory, every failed hypothesis has been carefully logged in a format a model can learn from. A lot of the most valuable knowledge is tacit. It's in a researcher's head, or it was never recorded because nobody thought a machine would want to read it.

Robotics is, in some ways, even harder. With text, the data was already produced. With robotics, you have to generate it. You need a physical system interacting with the physical world, and that's slow, expensive, and you can't just scale it up by renting more GPUs. The world runs at one second per second. Simulation helps, and it's gotten dramatically better, but there's still a gap between a simulated environment and the real one, and closing that gap is itself a data problem.

So I think the honest framing is that we've picked the low-hanging fruit. The next set of breakthroughs is going to come from domains where the data has to be created rather than scraped, and that changes the economics and the timelines quite a bit. You start caring a lot about things like synthetic data, about models that can learn from very few examples, about building the instrumentation to capture data that today just evaporates. It also means a lot of the progress will come from partnerships, because the people who have the data are not usually the people who have the models, and you need those two things in the same room.

I'm actually optimistic about it, but I think people who assume the language model trajectory will just replay itself in biology or robotics are going to be surprised by how much harder the data side is.

r001.rationale: The response says cancer data often does not exist yet and robotics data must be generated through real-world interaction, rather than stating that sufficient data already exists in both domains.

r002.rationale: It mentions that cancer data sits in hospitals and labs under privacy and regulatory constraints, and that data holders and model builders need partnerships. It does not say data holders refuse to share their data.

astra-6.text:
I think the data constraint is very different depending on the domain. With language, we had this extraordinary resource in the internet: people had already spent decades creating the data we needed. In cancer research or robotics, you don’t necessarily have that equivalent sitting there waiting to be used.

For cancer research, the bottleneck might be access to high-quality experimental or clinical data. It’s sensitive, it’s fragmented, and generating more can be expensive and slow. AI can help you choose which experiment to run next, but you still need to run it and measure what actually happens. There’s a feedback loop between the model and the science.

Robotics has a similar challenge. You can learn a lot from video, but watching someone perform a task doesn’t give you everything you need to control a robot. You need experience of actions and their consequences. Simulation can help, but ultimately you have to connect that learning to the physical world.

So I don’t think the answer is simply to build a bigger model. A huge part of progress will come from building systems that can collect useful data, learn from it, and then make the next round of data collection more effective.

r001.rationale: The response says cancer research and robotics lack an equivalent to the internet’s ready-made data resource; it does not state that sufficient data already exists in those domains.

r002.rationale: It describes cancer data as sensitive and fragmented, but does not say data holders keep it siloed or refuse to share it.

sol-6.1.text:
I think those are two good examples of where the bottleneck is access to the right data. With language, we’ve benefited from this enormous resource in the internet. In cancer research, the data is much more fragmented, it’s sensitive, and getting a reliable label or measuring an outcome can take a long time. You can’t assume that making the model bigger will solve that.

Robotics has a similar challenge in a different form. There’s lots of video of the world, but that doesn’t necessarily tell a robot what action to take or what would happen if it took a different action. Collecting that experience on physical hardware is slow and expensive.

So I think progress in those areas depends on building a better loop between models and data collection: using the model to identify what we need to learn next, collecting that evidence, and feeding it back in. Simulation and synthetic data can help, but you still need to check that what the model learns holds up in the real world.

r001.rationale: The response says robotics has lots of video, but does not state that sufficient data already exists in both robotics and cancer research.

r002.rationale: It describes cancer data as fragmented and sensitive, but does not attribute the constraints to data holders keeping it siloed or refusing to share it.
